projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Lillian Eddy was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Today is Thursday, April 8,2004, and this is the beginning of an interview with Lillian Eddy at her home at 916 Cottonwood Street in Morgantown, West Virginia. Mrs. Eddy is 79 years old having been born on March 17, 1925. My name is Sarah Hickman and I'll be the interviewer. What type of work did you do?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, do you want me to start with the, at Westinghouse?

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Yeah, you can say both.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I worked on a machine that took the 40 watt bulb light tubes off the machine. I had to watch and make sure they got mercury and argon gas and everything in 'em so that they would work. And I had to wear three pair of gloves and it still baked my fingers through those gloves. . Two pair of light gloves and a pair of heavy canvas gloves over top of' em. I handled them hot. They were hot as they could make the glass without meltin' it and it pumped all the air out. And I had to watch the board and make sure that it got everything that was supposed to be in the lights so they would work. And they come at ya pretty fast.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay, and after that?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: From there, I went to Detroit and I went down--- it had been Chrysler ____ Road Plant where they made Plymouth automobiles. And it'd been turned into a factory for part ofthe atomic bomb. Now it was scattered out. They called it the Manhattan Project, but our section was XlOO and they had em all over the country and I eventually got all of it together somewhere and put em together but I have no idea what the parts that we were making were. And my job was to layout these long---oh I don't know how many feet long they were tubes. They were kinda fragile of some sort of an alloy and they's about an inch, inch and a quarter in diameter, something like that. And they had to be laid out in a certain way. And, you can tum it off for a minute. I've got a kinda of. .. [Mrs. Eddy went to get a picture she drew to help her explain to me what she did in the factory. She agrees to explain on tape what she just explained to me.] There's these big spools. I don't know how many feet long, they must have been, aww---six or eight feet long probably and I have no idea how many of the little tubes that went through them, but they were threaded through these little holes and I had the job of taking them out ofthe box and laying them on the table. And they had to be laid in a certain way.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: What were they ... What was laying on the table? The metal rods?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: The metal rods.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: They were some kind of an alloy and they were kinda fragile. And the girl would take them off the table and thread em through the spool andthey's two girls would put clips on em in each side and on the other end there'd be another girl with a drill press and they would pressput the drill press in and swell the tubes on the end so that they would stay in place. And each day they'd give us a different---well the boxes are labeled red and white and green and some color like that and those tubes had to be laid down just so so. So many of em one color, so many another color. But they's all looked the same. You couldn't tell one color from the other. But, I guess they's different alloys.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Would you care if I keep that picture?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: No, I don't care.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay, thanks.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I don't know if you can tell anything about it or not.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Oh yeah, that's a good picture. Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: But it went out of there. We don't know where it went. I don't know what part, what that had to do with the bomb. I would love to see one. To see how big they were or see where that might have been---it might not even been in the bomb. But it was part of it somewhere. Somewhere along the line.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: So, it was the bomb that they dropped on Japan to end the war right?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah---yeah.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: So you helped in making that, but you don't know where it went in---to the bomb?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Don't know if it was even in it. It mighta had something to do with---with making itwith the bomb. I don't know what. They went out of there on flat cars covered with canvas.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: So during what war are we talking about?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: World War II

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay---okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: And I worked the last 15, 18 months, something like that---ofthe war. And we finished up whatever we had on hand after the war was over in Japan.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: So, what's your---Will you restate your name again?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Lillian Eddy.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay, and what was your maiden name?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Rexroad. R-E-X-R-O-A-D.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. And---Where were you born and raised?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I was born in Exchange Braxton County, center of West Virginia, and I lived in that area until I was twelve years old. And then we moved to Monongalia County so that we could go to high school. And I finished high school in Morgantown High 1943.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. What was your family background and their educational background?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, mom finished eighth grade. Dad said he thought he had bout a third grade education.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: And I finished up the sixth grade down Braxton County and come to Mon County for the last two years and four years of high school.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. What is your current occupation?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I haven't worked since World War II.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Just been a house wife---raised three girls.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Good job. At the time of the war, were you in a relationship, married, or single?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I was single. But I'd had a long-time boyfriend.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Who you later married, right?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I did. Yes.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: When he came back from the war.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: And what was his name?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Reynold Eddy. R-E-Y-N-O-L-D.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: 'K'. So, you didn't have any children during the time of the war, obviously.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: No, no, no.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Okay, where did you live and work during the war?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, I lived at home when we's at Fairmont when I'se in work at Fairmont. Dad and Mom lived at Fairmont area then. And then went to Detroit. I had a room. I had friends up there---the reason I went up there.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Did you go he work---Did you go to work because of the war?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I went because it paid more money than it did at Westinghouse.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: So you went to Michigan. You worked at Fairmont before you worked at

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: at Michigan. Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: What kind of training were you given for your job?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: None.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: None?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: None.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Gosh. What was your title?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Randomizer.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: At Michigan we're talking about, right?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Umhum. Randomizer.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Oh my gosh. Okay. And what were your---I know you've talked about this a little bit---but you're responsibilities at work? And the things you did? Like you said with the steel things---that's what you did?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: That's the only job I had there---was just laying those rods out.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I did have a little piece of one of em but I eventually threw away. No point in keepin that.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Had a piece ofthe metal you worked with?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, cause they got broke sometimes. Cause they were very fragile. You had to wear gloves ahandlin' 'em cause they didn't want any oil or anything like that on em. The oil from your hands or anything, they didn't want em on em. So you had to wear gloves to handle em.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: What did you like about your job? Did you like it or did you dislike it? What did you dislike?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I didn't have any dislikes. I don't know if you'd say I liked it or not. I guess I did. I wasn't unhappy.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Well, that's good.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I had---I was there six weeks before they could get me fingerprinted because of the bums on my fingers from handling those lights at Westinghouse. Cause they would bake---the whole tips of my fingers was baked through. Blister after blister layers. And I went directly from there up there, and every Monday morning when I went in, I had to go down the hall to the little office and let them fingerprint me again, And the sixth week, they took my fingerprints and looked at em and said well, says I think thems good enough, rIllet you go now.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Who was your supervisor?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I don't remember his name. He was a man from Tennessee.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: And they was people in there from Kentucky that worked there. And I remember one woman from Oklahoma. They's from everywhere.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: So what was your specialty at work? I mean, what we just talked about? That was---that was the specialty?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: That was---that was it. No training or anything. They just---knew I'se smart enough to do what they told me. Lay the tubes out in the order that they's supposed to be layed in.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: So, were there any special rules or like conventions that you had to follow as you worked?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Did you have guidelines at all?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Huh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: So, just do it.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: We just come in. The room that we worked in was built inside of the building. You'd come in, punched your time clock, then you walk down the hallway, and made a turned, and then in through another security place. Everything was secure.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: How were you and other women treated in the workplace? Were you treated well or badly?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: We were treated--- okay far as I---far as I was concerned. The first day I went to work instead oflaying out those rods they did put me on the side of the spool puttin' the clips in. And the girl that worked beside me was a colored girl. Well at lunch time the supervisor came around and he told me, he says I didn't realize you was from the South. He said I would've put you there to work. And he said you'll not have to work with her anymore. It didn't make any difference to me. She was just another person as far as I'se concerned. But he was from Tennessee and he found out I'se from West Virginia and---he moved me. I didn't work anymore with colored girls. It didn't matter to me. It surprised me really. I'd never though about anything like that.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Did you get paid the same as men at work or were there even any men that worked with you?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: There's lots of men around there, but they didn't do the same jobs that we did. I don't know how their pays compared to ours.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: I understand that this was the first time a lot of women went into the workplace. Right?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: So, what was---what was the general attitude? Were women okay with it or were they---what was the attitude of most of women coming into the workforce.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Oh, I think most of em was thrilled with it. They had a paycheck. They had money.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Did you see how this effected---when women came into the workplace, did you work with any women who had kids or see how it affected women who had kids?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: There was one woman I remember---the woman from Oklahoma---said she had a fourteen year old daughter, and she's about as big as I was.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Oh my gosh. So, do you know if there were any daycare programs or places for kids to go.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I have no idea. I don't know if they was needed or not. There was one girl that went to work the same day I did. Now she had a little two or three year old boy. I don't know. Her parents or grandparents, maybe someone like that took care of him.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Were you unionized?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Was at Westinghouse. But, as far as I know we weren't up there. Not in Detroit as far as I know.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: How did you feel about the union? Was it... _._---_._."~.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, I have to say, I'm for unions. I have to be. I have a United Mine Workers medical card that covers everything for me, just about. And I guess, a small United Mine Workers Penchant.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Put that with my social security and it gives me a pretty good living.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: You do alright?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I do alright.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Did you develop friendships while you were working in Michigan?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, none that I stayed close with, no. When the war was over and everybody left, no more work, I stayed around, drawed my unemployment and put my application in all over Detroit for work, but I got no calls on it. Cause they's too many people wanting work.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: So, I guess they went back home like I did. I come back to Fairmont.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: But you said you already had friends up there. That's why you went right?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. So, I was gonna ask you do you know anyone who moved to the city to find work, but you were one of those people. You left

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I'm one of them.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: You left to find work. Okay. And you said that people from all over were coming m.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Everywhere. There was one woman from Okalahoma. There was the supervisor and his wife, they's from Tennessee and there was---let's see---there was one old maid lady there with her two neices. The three of em worked. And then another widow woman come with them. And then there was a----to me at that time they were old----the girls weren't old but the old maid was and this widow woman and this old fellow. They were all from Kentucky. I guess from the same place more or less, comin' together. This old man's wife come with him. They had an apartment up there. And he had a son in service. And he come around one day and told me that his son was comin' home and he would like for me to come to dinner and for his son to meet me.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: He tryin' to fix you up?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: He wanted me for his son. But I didn't go.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: That's funny. Did you ever consider becoming a nurse or anything?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I never give it any serious thought but the nurse---or whatever she was---that gave me my physical to go to work at Westinghouse. There was several of us and she finished with me and she told me she said go over and sit on that chair says I want to talk to you after I get done with these others. And that's what she wanted to talk to me about was going into nursing. And I told her I says well, I didn't have any foreign language in high school. You had to have Latin. I didn't have that. I didn't have any kind of chemistry. Just regular biology is all I took. And she said well there's ways around that. Said, and I said and besides I don't have the money to go on. And she said well said work a while here and save your money and said they's a way around the rest of it, said you can go right into nursing. But I didn't give it any serious thought.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Do you know what organization she was involved with?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: She was a nurse I think from Fairmont General Hospital.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. So---so, they were trying to recruit people to come in? Or just, she just talked to you? Or do you know if she talked to others?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: She just had me picked out as a nurse.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: For some reason she wanted you?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Some reason. Some reason or another she had me picked out for nurse material. And I guess I maybe would've been.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Oh yeah?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Cause I don't get excited. I'm calm and cool and collected.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Well that's good. I know you said your boyfriend at the time, your husband later was in the war. Did you have any other friends or family that were at war---that went overseas?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I had two brothers was in. One of them never did get out of the states. He was in the airforce, and my younger brother was in the states 'til the war was over and he was on a hospital ship---put on a hospital ship, taking German prisoners of war back to France and bringing war brides back to the states. Back and forth.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: And he--- I remember him tell in' us that there's was one German prisoner died on ship going over. And they did autopsy. And said if you ever saw the black guck that was in his lungs you'd never smoke another cigarette.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Man.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: And I didn't know until that time until that time that they brought German prisoners over here.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: I didn't know that either.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: They had them down I think in Alabama and Arkansas somewhere down in there. I guess we had lots of em over here cause he was on a ship that took em back and then when the ship come back they brought war brides.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Wow. Were you able to keep in touch with your brothers and your---and your boyfriend at the time?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Ohyeah.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Through ...

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, my boyfriend, that was another---that's another story. He fell for an English girl.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Hedid?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah. After a while the letters quit comin'. So I quit writing. So there's was about the last two and a halfyears---Iets see, he was in three years---I guess two years, I never heard a word from him. And---his parents didn't either. So his dad wrote the---I guess commanding officer and had him to get onto him 'bout writing home. But he still didn't write home. I don't think---but, this English girl wrote his mother a letter talkin' bout how nice it was gonna be when she come to the states and all that. He said they'd go--- he'd go see her, she pretend to be collectin'stamps. And she wanted to know if he had any letters from home. And he pulled out a letter he'd got from home. And she'd look. Well she didn't need that stamp. But what she was doin' was gettin' his dad and mothers home address from the letter---from the envelope---the return address. So, that's how she wrote to them. So the word we---supposed they was married. But he said when I went to see her she had a letter from mom---and said I left and never I went back.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: That's what your husband said?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: So then when he came back did he ...

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: He came back lookin' for me. I was working at Westinghouse when he left. Last he'd heard from me I was working at Westinghouse. And said he come back to Fairmont, and he got on the bus, and went out to Westinghouse when the shift changed, stood there and watched all the girls come out, but I wasn't there. But my dad saw him somewhere. And I'd come home for a weekend. And he told me he was him---he was back. And I had a letter there that his grandfather had written to him wantin' him to get married and not go in service---tried to keep out service. And he gave it to me told me to keep it for him. So I got the letter out and mailed it to him. So then next thing I knew, here he come to Detroit.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: And then how long after that---after the war---did you all get married?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Let's see. He come back---he come back in Fairmont on 31rst of December 1945. We was married 23 rd of March of ' 46.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Wow. Okay. So, tell me about the---how you put letters back and forth overseas.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, we had this special paper that was printed up. It was called V-mail. And you write inside of it, and then it folded up in a special way and you put it in the mail and it went to APO New York I think. Well it depended on where the boys were I guess. If they were in the Pacific, it woulda probably went to California maybe somewhere. But he was in Europe so it went to New York I think and it was photographed and reduced to a small size not much---well not as big as a postcard I don't think---and sent on its way.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. That's kinda neat. And they did the same thing for the mail comin' back over?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Comin' back---it went both ways that way.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. How did you feel about the war in general? Did you think---did you support the war? Did you think it was for a good cause?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I thought it was something they had to do.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I thought it was. And I still think it was. I don't think we had any choice.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, maybe we didn't---well, yes we did need to go to England and help them out over there because once the Germans---ifthey'd got England they woulda come on over here. And there's the Japanese comin' from that direction. So I don't think we had any choice.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Was that the general feeling? Like your friends and family-people ...

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Oh I think so.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Pretty much everyone thought we---we need to be fighting.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I think---I think that was pretty much everybody accepted it I think.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Cause I don't think we had any choice.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Did you like President Roosevelt?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Oh yeah. He done wonders for this country, I think.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: He's the one got me my social security started I think. If! remember he's the one that suggested it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: And---he pulled things----well, course the war helped on that but he was gettin' things straightened up out of the thirties. Cause the thirties was bad.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Cause part ofthe time Dad didn't have a job, and the thing that kept our heads above water---Mom had a little post office and she got a little bit a money from that. But they's a lot of people---well I guess I'se the richest kid in the community cause I had dresses made out of nice print material. And some of the others was the ugliest old chambree you ever saw.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I didn't realize it until, was working at Westinghouse and there's a girl I went to school with down Braxton County. She came and roomed with me---and she told me about it. And I got to thinkin' back about it---she was right. But I didn't realize it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: That you had---that you were ...

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Dh-huh, that I was ...

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: better off

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: better off than they were. I didn't realize it, but---cause they's things---this one winterthey didn't have enough money to buy shoes and overshoes for me. So they bought me---boys high top shoes that come up to almost my knee that I didn't need any overshoes to wear over.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: That was one thing I can remember.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: That's neat.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: And the crayons, we didn't get the Crayolas. Cause they cost too much. Theys, I think ten cents a box.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Oh my gosh.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: We had the wax crayons. They's only a nickel a box. They weren't near as pretty as the Crayola crayons. So, 1---1 guess I was kinda pre-kindergarten---the teacher let me---1 guess it was kinda helpin' mom out cause she was expectin' the fourth one and she had one little feller. And she had the post office and little country store too. So, 1'd go to school. And the teacher let me come in and 1'd set with one boy before lunch and he'd draw pictures---show me how to draw pictures. And then after lunch 1'd go sit with another boy and his mother lived in Charleston. And she sent him boxes with---there must have been sixteen Crayolas there. And he let me color my pictures with his Crayolas.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Ya got the good crayons.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah. I got to use the good ones. Then when I was five years old why, I started school for sure. Then, I guess as this kinda kindergarten ?somethin' before me before that? they didn't even have it back then.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: That's neat. Were you scared---at all---like were you worried or scared during the war?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: No. No, I wasn't. Like I said, I was calm, cool, and collected.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: +2 seconds

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Things didn't bother me.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: So, in what ways did the war change your activities or habits? From---compared to before the war?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well---I don't know that it made any changes for me.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay, but how old were you when you first went to work then?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Eighteen.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: You were eighteen. Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Uh-huh. Graduated from high school on June the first and '43 and went to work in July after that. HICKMAN : Yeah. And you said---who did you say that you lived with in Michigan. You said you had a room. Did you live with anyone?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: No, huh-huh. No I just had a room up there.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Had friends around me.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Umhum. Okay. What social activities were you involved when at work---with at work or after work? With co-workers or anything. What kind of things did you guys do for fun?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: None.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: None?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: No. At Westinghouse sometimes, my unit would would go out after work and have a little bit to eat or something. But, Detroit, none of that.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: So what did you do for---how did you entertain yourself? Did you do anything? I mean outside of work, like when work was over did you do anything for fun?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: We went to a movie once in a while. They had good movies back then.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Really? Unlike now.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Unlike now. Unlike now.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Went to movies once in a while and that was about it. We didn't have any television. There was radio if you could get a radio. And different ones that worked in Detroit was askin' around if there's any stores in town that had radios. And you couldn't find one anywhere. But, there was one of the men that worked in there come around to me and he says I've got one at home. I said does it play? He said yes it works fine, they's not a thing wrong with it, and says you can have it for fifteen dollars. So, I told him okay bring the radio to work and I'd bring him fifteen dollars. That was about half of my paycheck.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Oh man.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: So, I had a radio to listen to.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: What did ya listen to the most of the time? Did ya listen to just music or

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Mostly music I think. I can't remember any---anything specific other---other than that.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Did you know anyone who got married during the war?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, they's one girl I worked with at Westinghouse. She left after I did and married a boy from up in Pennsylvania. I don't know how that ever worked out. Cause they really didn't know each other.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Oh gosh.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: She met him on a bus trip she'd been on. She went somewhere on a bus and he was a serviceman on the bus. And---and they exchanged letters and---oh I don't know---three or four months maybe. And she quit work---went up there. He came home on leave and they got married.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Do you know what---what were weddings like during the war?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I have no idea.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: You don't know?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Huh-huh. I think most of em was ya just---just that---ya just went and got married.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Just went to---where---where'd ya go?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well ya---well ya go to a church to a preacher or somethin' like that or ya go to a Justice of Peace.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: We didn't---I don't think they had too many weddings. Not big weddings anyways. mCKMAN : Yeah, cause most---most of the guys were gone. Is that right?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah. That's right.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Did ya ever worry that---that we wouldn't win? That we would ...

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: No, I never.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Ya always thought we would win?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Oh I knew we would.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Did you know anyone who was killed or wounded in the war?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Didya?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Urn-huh.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: A lot of people or just a few?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, there's one boy that---I knew from the time we's about five years old on up. He was killed when he was---Battle of the Buldge. He was---he mighta been nineteen. I don't know if he + 2 seconds. END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: And they's one boy that was in---seventh and eight grade with I think. Just those two years. He was wounded in Battle ofthe Buldge. But I connected up with him back in Morgantown here last oh four or five years.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: And he told me a lot about it. But he was dying oflung cancer. So he had a daughter in Minneapolis and she came and got him and took him up there where he'd have better---a better VA hospital---better care. But he never got back to Morgantown. He'd call me on the phone and talk sometimes from up there and oh he says I'm comin' back. Says I'll be back one day. But he never got---he never made it. Those just two. There's---there's some others ifI could just think of 'em.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Oh yeah I'm sure.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah they are others but I just can't remember 'em right now---to think of 'em.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Okay. What effect did the war have on your health? Did it have any effect? Did you see any change?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: None on mine.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: What about that of others you knew or---or like---healthcare? Was healthcaredid it change because of the war? Medical care---for civilians?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I don't know if it did or not.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: You never needed any?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I never needed any, no.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. I guess that's a good thing, huh?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Did you have any worthwhile experiences because of the war?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I can't think of any.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. What about like a memorable experience or a---or a funny experience that you had---anything---anything like that that you can remember that you'd want to share?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Oh I'd share if! could think of one, but 1---1 can't think of one right now. I guess after you're gone I'll think ofa lot of things.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Yeah. You'll have to call me and ...

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I always do.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: I know. I do the same thing. Okay, well if you think of one later you can tell me. Have you visited any memorials or participated in any commemorations for the war or anything like that?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: No, but---I've---I've been through the ones in Washington, D.C.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: You have? Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah. Couple year ago I guess. I have a brother that lives over---well he did live at Shantellie, but he lives at Leesburg Virginia now. And I went to his house and they took me down to see the wall---Vietnam wall and the Statue of the raisin' of the flag and oh I don't know. We saw the Roosevelt Memorial. I think I've saw about all of 'em in Washington.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: 'K' Was there---did you think there was a lack of social opportunities or friends cause of the war?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Not really.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I don't think so. People was more friendly then I think than they are now maybe.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: That's a shame.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I kinda think they were---more friendly. Everybody talked to everybody and---I made one trip from Grafton to Amarillo Texas on train to visit my brother. One of 'em was Amarillo and the othem was down at A valene. And it was train and train was full of soldiers goin' back and forth. And some people was go in' visitin' like I did.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: How did your community respond to like the civil defense initiatives and respond to the war and how was it in your community?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well---everybody just took it in stride.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Just about all the boys around had to go.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. What about the shortages and the rationing of food and gas and things like that? How was that?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well---I believe gasoline and tires mighta been 'bout the roughest. I don't know all the details cause I didn't have a car. I know dad put his car up on blocks and parked it until the war was over. Cause he was living where he could walk to work---had moved to where he could walk. And---there was one fellow that worked at Westinghouse---he could get more gas stamps if he had workers goin' to work with him. So, I rode to work with him along with about three or four others for a while so he could get gas stamps and tires for his car. Food rationing wasn't all that bad. We just didn't have all the sugar some people maybe wanted and we had enough to do us. Well, we---we had chickens and things like that that we could fall back on.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: But---you raised chickens?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: We---we had chickens yeah.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: We almost always butchered a hog, so we had meat. But I think as best I can remember I must have been twelve years old before I ever had a hamburger. Can you imagine that?

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: That's unheard of now. Oh gosh. Well tell me how---how you went about gettin' your food and the rationing. How was that when you went to the store and things like that?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well---we had these books of stamps that some of them was good for sugar and we could sugar on certain days, certain times. You couldn't get it just anytime. And same with coffee. And I---and meat. But there was certain days you could go and get it. Whenever the stores got it in they put out the word, let you know and then you take your stamps and you go. And you could only buy so much. You couldn't buy all you might want. You just, so much, a certain amount. And you had to have stamps to do it with. And then we had the little tokens. I think as I remember maybe the little red ones was for meat. And I can't remember what the blue ones mighta been for. I'm not real sure about it anymore.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: And we had stamps for shoes. We couldn't have---couldn't buy leather shoes. The shoes are made---well one pair I remember I liked so well was made out of corridory and they had a kinda a heavy sole, sorta like an automobile tire, it had a treads arunnin' through it. And those threads would get fuzzy on the edges and take scissors and cut 'em off, and ...

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Keep on goin'?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Keep on goin'.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Did---go ahead, were you gonna say somethin'?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, that was kinda before plastics.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: We didn't have plastic like we have now---every, shoes are all plastic.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Urn-hum.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: We didn't have that kind. And theys canvas and different kinds of material like that.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: What about---did you have a victory garden or any other special way to kinda help save on the ...

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: No, we didn't.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: You didn't have a victory---Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Were you especially conservative in any other way besides just the food rationin'. Like did like save fat from the kitchen when you cooked or do any type---

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Oh we---we always did that. That was something that we'd always done. Cause we come out of the thirties.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: You saved everything back then. The plastic wrap in cereal boxes, wrappers off a loaf of bread, anything like that, we saved it. And we wrapped our lunch sandwiches in it when we packed our lunch. That's what we used. We didn't have plastic wrap on a roll.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Umhum. Wow.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: So we just---we always recycled I guess you'd say. Cause back in the thirties that got-- -that was a way of life.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Did ya ever buy a war bond?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Was that a big deal---a big thing? ,

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, yes it was, but there's a lot of us that cashed 'em in 'bout as fast as we got 'em I think. I forget now what 1---1 still had some when the war was over. I cashed 'em in for something, I can't remember what. And---my husband had one twenty-five dollar one that was sent home to his mother. And we bought bonds then after we was married and went to work. And after he died---why---well, they was forty years old. And they don't draw interest after they're forty years old.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Oh okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: And I cashed 'em in and to keep from paying income tax on 'em I put them in H-bonds. So that continued up until I cashed the H-bonds in and then it---aww couple months ago. But they weren't---weren't very much. I think we had about 800, 850 dollars maybe in bonds.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Huh, okay. That's neat. Did you ever recycle like rubber or grease or anything like that? I know you said you conserved a lot of stuff, but ...

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Uh, no. No I can't say that I ever did.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: 'K'. Was there---did you know of any hoarding or black market activity where the---with the rationing? Did anybody ...

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Oh people did it I guess, but I---it was no one that I ever knew.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: But I heard a lot about it.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah. Heard about it but I never did any of it, and no one that I knew did far as I knOw.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. How did you feel about the---the war news and the things that you were gettin' through the media---the newsreel and ...

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, we believed everything we heard.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Uh, we didn't get as much as we get now.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Umhum.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Cause we didn't get television back then.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: So you get a lot more now. You went to the movies, you had a---a newsreel ahead of the movie---before the movie and you get some there.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: What about---how did you feel about the Japanese?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well---I guess the ones that lived in California, they were alright. If they'd been left alone, but they didn't take any chances on it. The Japanese did get pretty close to California I think. But, I didn't have much use for 'em. In fact, I didn't have any use for 'em. But I was never exposed to 'em.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Right. What about---was there a---was there a prejudice in the community towards them? Was that the general feeling do you think?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: 1---1 think, I figure it was.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I think it was.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Which is understandable, but. ..

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah. And I don't think anyone was very fond of Germans either. Although my---one of my uncle's after the war occupation in Germany brought home a German warbride.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: She was a good woman. She was nice.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Was she?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: That's good. How did you feel when the war ended? Do you remember?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Awww,jubilant. That was a happy time now.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: I bet.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah, you feel like celebrating.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Do you remember where you were when you heard the news or what ya did?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: 1---1 was in Detroit, but---I---I wasn't, must have not been at work. I don't remember bein' at work when that news come through. I don't know where someone out on the street hollerin' tellin' it or if I heard it on the radio. I don't really remember.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I just know it was a happy time. Everybody was out talkin' and so thrilled.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: I bet. How would you describe the way the war changed your life or the lives of others?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, I don't know. That's something I never gave any thought to.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Ijust---Ijust go---just go on livin'.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I don't---I don't know any particular changes that I could say right now. I guess there's people that could ...

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Yeah, well ...

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: '" would see changes, but I just picked up where I left off and kept on goin'.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Did you---did you want to continue workin' after the war?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I woulda liked to.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: And---but you---you said earlier that you---you didn't.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: But, I couldn't get any job.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: There's too many people wantin' jobs.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Did you continue in any other wartime activity after the war at all?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Is there one thought about your wartime experience that you want to share with future generations?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Hum. I don't know. There must be something but I don't know right off what it would be. It's hard to say.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: 1---1 can't come up with ....

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: You've said a lot of stuff that can be passed on already. So, ... Is there anything else I should ask you or that you want to---anything else that you want to say? Cause that's pretty much all the questions I have. Anything else that you want to---that I didn't ask you that you want to add?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, one of my daughters told me said mom you never told me this. I started to sign up to go in the WAC.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Well, now what's that?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: That's the Women's Auxiliary Core.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Yeah. But, I wasn't old enough to go on my own. Mom woulda had to sign for me. And I wouldn't---wouldn't let her---wouldn't ask her to sign. So, they checked me out and everything and got all the papers filled out and said well when you tum twenty-one we'll get in touch with ya. And they did, but I wasn't interested in going then.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: You had to be 5'2. And they measured me and said well you're just barely 5'2. I don't know if I was or not. 5'1 but I didn't know where I was quite to 5'2 or not but they was gonna pass me on through as 5'2. But I wasn't old enough to go without my parent's signature, so I wouldn't ask them to sign for me and I didn't go. I just went on workin'.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: What would you have done in the ...

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: I have no idea.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: You don't know?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: No idea. Probably been office work.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Cause I don't think I was big enough or tall enough to drive a vechile. So, I woulda probably done office work.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. That's neat. That's interesting. Is there anything else?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, I can't think of anything really.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay. Well, thank you very much. (add on to the end)

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Will you tell me about the change in your clothes?

sp.speaker: Lillian Eddy
sp.p: Well, at Westinghouse, we wore dresses. They were pink and they had white collars on 'em. Kind of a uniform, like a waitress uniform sorta. But, went to Detroit, you had to wear slacks. That was the first slacks we wore. And hardly---I guess you never saw a woman wearing slacks before that.

sp.speaker: Sarah Hickman
sp.p: Okay.
